title: Fast & Slow Pointers: Find the Middle of a Linked List
oneLiner: Two pointers moving at different speeds down the SAME list -- when the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is sitting exactly at the middle.
keyTakeaway: Fast & slow (Floyd's) pointers solve "where's the middle" and "is there a cycle" without ever counting the list's length first -- fast moves two steps for every one the slow pointer takes, so by the time fast has covered the whole list, slow has covered exactly half of it.
explanation:
The obvious way to find a linked list's middle node is two passes: walk the whole list once to count its length n, then walk again to node n/2. Fast & slow pointers do it in ONE pass: start both pointers at the head, then loop advancing slow by one node and fast by two nodes each iteration, stopping the moment fast reaches the end (or has no next node left to jump to). Because fast always covers exactly twice the distance slow does, the moment fast has traveled the full list, slow has traveled exactly half of it -- sitting right at the middle, no length-counting required.

This exact same "two speeds, one pass" idea also detects a CYCLE in a linked list (Floyd's cycle detection): if the list loops back on itself instead of ending, the fast pointer eventually LAPS the slow pointer and they land on the same node again -- if that ever happens, there's a cycle; if fast reaches a real null ending first, there isn't one. Both problems are the identical mechanism pointed at two different questions.

Watch the two pointers below advance at their different speeds -- slow (blue) takes one step at a time; fast (amber) takes two, and the walkthrough stops the instant fast can't safely take another full 2-step hop.

recognitionSignals: The problem is about a linked list's MIDDLE, or about detecting a CYCLE/loop, and you'd otherwise need to know the list's length up front.
You need an answer in one pass without a separate length-counting pass first.
gotchas: The stopping condition has to check BOTH "fast isn't null" AND "fast's next isn't null" before advancing fast by two -- checking only one crashes on some odd-vs-even-length lists.
For an even-length list this lands on the SECOND of the two middle nodes by convention -- double check which middle a problem actually wants if it matters.
